1:
Henry and Wesley note how strange the order was. A stage or two more would have brought them to Horeb, the place appointed for their serving God; instead they are told to turn short off, away from Canaan, towards the sea. At Etham no water lay in their path, so it was God himself who put them into straits — which, Henry adds, might have assured them that when his purposes were served he would as surely bring them out, since he sometimes raises difficulties in his people's way that he may have the glory of subduing them. Keil grants the turn was not out of the way for a passage through the sea, but by human reckoning it was a foolish one. Ellicott plots it: the march had run almost south-east to the head of the Bitter Lakes, and the command turned them south, keeping them inside Egypt with the Lakes now on their left. He rejects the rendering of the verb as a command to retrace their steps, since the march was to bring them to a sea they had not yet reached, and rejects the Mediterranean, which Exodus never calls simply the sea.

The three place-names are worked over and not settled. Clarke takes Pi-hahiroth for the mouth or bay of Chiroth, Migdol for the tower, probably a fortress guarding the bay, and Baal-zephon for the lord of the watch, likely a temple with a light kept as a mark for shipping. Calvin works at the etymology and gives it up honestly: he prefers a root meaning to engrave, since the rocks look cut as with a mallet — but the word mouth makes it certain the defile was narrow and rock-walled, with the sea closing the other side, as though Israel had been laid in a sepulchre. Ellicott holds all three unidentifiable, small places near the head of the Gulf of Suez, and turns it into evidence: so many obscure names argue a knowledge of Egyptian ground no Israelite is likely to have had who had not walked it. Gill cites a traveller on the breach in the range by which one may turn short off into the valley of Baideah and follow it to the sea.

On the entanglement the commentators agree and press it hard. Clarke sets out the position: the sea in front, Pharaoh behind, fortresses to right and left, and not one boat prepared — so that if they were saved at all the arm of the Lord must be seen and the Egyptian gods shown to be nothing. Ellicott renders the word confused or perplexed and reads it from Pharaoh's side, who saw them marching south with the desert before them and thought they had lost their way. Calvin settles on confounded, since they could find no way out; Wesley has them shut in by mountains and deserts; and Keil gives Pharaoh's thought as a prison whose door is shut.

Henry reads the disclosure as a courtesy: Moses is told that Pharaoh has a design to ruin Israel and God therefore a design to ruin Pharaoh, using the king's own shrewdness against him, for the deeper the entanglement looked the readier he would be to come on. Since all men are made for their Maker's honour, those he is not honoured by he will be honoured upon. Calvin makes the same point as strategy, that God set a bait to catch the tyrant as a fish is hooked: had Israel walked out peaceably the earlier miracles would not have testified their redemption sufficiently, whereas being shut in and seeing nothing but death they had to confess themselves saved by God's hand from the abysses. Clarke has God withdraw restraining grace and let the king rush on; Keil holds that what turned the king's heart was not the change of route but the flight itself, which left him time to muster chariots.
5:
What exactly was reported, and why it changed the king's mind, is answered four ways. Clarke points out that Pharaoh cannot have been ignorant of the departure, having licensed it; fled must mean they had gone for good, which he had not expected, having granted only three days' journey — and what weighed most with an avaricious king was the property carried off and the service lost. Wesley says he would not own that they went with his consent, being willing to have it represented as a revolt. Ellicott reckons the cost in economic terms: the emigration left eastern Egypt a solitude, suspended the royal works and threw commerce into disorder, neither king nor people having understood what the loss of six hundred thousand labourers would mean. Calvin denies that the flight was news at all, since it had been anything but secret; what was reported were the circumstances, and hearing they fled in haste the king judged the slightest obstacle might hold them. He is hardest on the courtiers, who blame their own inertness as though they had not been ten times overcome — the stupidity of the wicked, who dread only God's present hand and forget all they have seen.

Calvin reads the muster the same way: only the day before the Egyptians were frightened almost to death and crying that all was over, and now they collect an army as though their forces were untouched, which shows with what obstinate audacity the wicked go forward. He answers the obvious objection, that six hundred chariots were no match for six hundred thousand men, by observing that they expected an unwarlike crowd with women and children mixed in it; nor would they have been disappointed, had God not been against them. Ellicott notes that kings of that period almost always led their armies in person, and that made ready means ordered to be made ready — which is Gill's point too.

The chariot force is examined. Gill takes them for war chariots of iron, perhaps fitted with scythes to cut men down, chosen partly for speed, to overtake a people several marches ahead, and partly for strength. Clarke describes the crew: two or four horses and three men aboard, of whom the driver seldom fought, the second shielded him, and the third alone was properly the combatant. Ellicott sets the number against what is known: the largest well-attested muster is under four thousand, so six hundred chosen chariots is credible, most likely a division of the royal guard. He adds that all the chariots of Egypt must not be pressed, and that the captains were set over the whole force rather than over each — which Wesley reads the same way, command distributed among several captains.

On Israel's going out Ellicott would render the verb were going out, and takes the high hand for confidence and boldness, perhaps a touch of pride, as of men who had brought the Egyptians to beg them to leave; Wesley has it boldly and resolutely. Calvin hears a reproof in it: their security had freed them from all care, and the desire of calling on God had cooled with it, since safety breeds drowsiness, so that the danger, coming unlooked for, produced the greater fear — we should repose humbly under God's wings rather than be lifted up with inconsiderate joy. Of the pursuing force Ellicott defends the word horsemen against those who make it the riders in the chariots, since it is the one Hebrew word with that sense and there is abundant testimony that Egypt used cavalry, whatever the sculptures show. He takes the army that follows for the infantry, so the host had all three arms; Wesley thinks the king took no foot at all, his business requiring haste. Keil closes with the sight that met Israel, the Egyptian army advancing, and their great alarm.
10:
Henry and Wesley describe the trap in the same words: numerous indeed, but all on foot, unarmed, undisciplined and dispirited by long servitude, with impassable rocks on one hand, forts on the other, the sea in front and the Egyptians behind, so no way lay open but upwards — and thence their deliverance came. Ellicott meets the objection that six hundred thousand men had no business fearing Pharaoh's hasty levy. Herodotus puts Egypt's whole armed strength at four hundred and ten thousand, and not half could have been mustered; but numbers were not the point, since the Egyptians were trained and well-armed and the Israelites were neither. A million Persians were slaughtered like sheep by forty-seven thousand at Arbela, so the fear was legitimate. Calvin adds that the suddenness made it worse, no messenger going before.

What they did with the fear divides them. Henry separates two responses: some cried to the Lord, their fear setting them praying, since God brings us into straits that he may bring us to our knees; others cried out against Moses. Clarke reports Calmet's version of the division, the pious appealing to God while the irreligious murmured, and observes that had the prayer been joined with faith we should not find them murmuring next. Calvin refuses the division: the two statements stand together in one sentence and cannot be assigned to different people. On his reading the cry came neither from faith nor from ordered affection but was forced out by a confused impulse, since nature drives all men in trouble to pray without embracing God's mercy or relying on his power; and the wild cries against Moses are the proof that the calling on God had been thoughtless. Gill takes the middle ground: the Targum confines the murmur to the ungodly of that generation, but he judges the body of the people meant.

The murmur is read as irony. Ellicott makes the question about graves a bitter jest meaning that they might as well have died in Egypt as here, and calls the reproach unjust, since in the main they had acquiesced in Moses' proceedings and let him act in their name. Calvin sharpens it: not content with preferring Egyptian graves to the death they feared, they scoff as though Egypt had not room to bury them, forgetting that they had themselves been brought miraculously out of the grave. Henry finds in it a sordid contempt of liberty, when it were better to live God's freemen in the open air of a wilderness than the Egyptians' bondmen in the smoke of the brick-kilns; and he counts this the first of the ten provocations for which Israel was sentenced to die in the wilderness.

On the answer Moses gave, Henry and Wesley admire the restraint — he answered not these fools according to their folly, but instead of chiding comforted them, disheartened neither by the threatenings of Egypt nor the tremblings of Israel; it is our duty, when we cannot get out of our troubles, to get above our fears. Calvin doubts the silence: he thinks it improbable that Moses let such cries pass unrebuked, and conceives he chastised their insolence, omitting the reproof from his narrative only to show that God's kindness outran their impiety; stand still he glosses as keep quiet, no man having occasion to move a finger. Clarke agrees that no resistance was intended, since of that there was no hope: they were not even to be workers together with God, but to see a deliverance worked without them. Keil confirms the sense against the Greek: the words are inverted, and mean not that they would see them in that manner but that they would never see them again. Gill reads the fighting of the Lord concretely, by commanding the wind and the waves; Clarke, that they should have no part in the honour of the day.
15:
That God asks why Moses cries when no word of his praying is reported is noticed first. Henry and Wesley take it that he lifted up his heart without speech, and that these silent prayers of faith prevailed more than Israel's loud outcries of fear; the question is no rebuke but a dismissal — why press a petition already granted, with the hosts of Israel to command? Clarke turns it to the comfort of the inarticulate: the heart was deeply engaged though probably not a word was formed, and the language of sighs and tears is as intelligible to God as speech — a man who cannot pray may weep, and if tears are denied him may sigh. Gill takes it for mental prayer without voice, proving that assurance had not made Moses neglect the means; Keil says the words carry no reproof but an admonition to resolute action. Calvin rejects the reading that extends the question to the whole people, whose prayers were not directed to God at all: Moses had prayed apart, and the answer means only, weary yourself with crying no more.

On the order to go forward, Henry and Wesley report a suggestion that Moses had prayed less for the deliverance, of which he was sure, than for the pardon of the murmuring, so that the command was itself the intimation of pardon. They looked to be turned right or left; instead they are sent straight to the sea-side, as though a fleet of transports lay ready for them. Calvin adds that those are rash who promise particular blessings without a special word from God, Moses having proclaimed nothing he had not first heard.

The rod and the hardening go together. Gill notes it was the same rod that had done so many wonders in Egypt. Clarke observes that neither Moses nor his rod could effect anything in a work belonging to omnipotence alone, but that he had to appear in it so Israel might see whom God had chosen. Henry and Wesley add that the same power could have frozen the waters to pass over, but infinite wisdom chose rather to divide them to pass through, the way of salvation always pitched upon being the most humbling. Henry weighs the emphatic I, behold I three ways — sovereignty, since God's grace is his own; power, since none but the Almighty can make a heart soft and no other can make it hard; and justice, it being righteous to put men under his wrath who have long resisted his grace. Calvin uses the verse against the doctrine of bare permission: the Egyptians would never have dared enter a sea plainly armed against them unless God had blinded them.

The moving of the pillar is read as guard and emblem. Henry and Wesley have the angel leave the front, where a guide was no longer wanted, for the rear, where a guard was; there it lit Israel through the water and confounded the pursuers, who lost sight of their prey as they were about to lay hands on it — the word and providence of God having a dark side towards sinners and a bright one towards Israelites indeed. Clarke describes the cloud's two faces, the luminous lighting the camp all the night of the passage and the dark denying the Egyptians any benefit of it. Who the angel was they answer alike. Clarke allows that a cloud so appointed might be called a messenger, but thinks the Angel of the covenant appeared; Gill accepts the Jewish identification with Michael only if the uncreated Word is meant; Calvin observes that he who has been called Jehovah throughout is here called the Angel, and takes him for the only-begotten Son. He adds the corollary that the glory which enlightens the faithful darkens unbelievers, so it is no wonder if the brightness of the Gospel blinds the reprobate still.
21:
Henry sets the dividing of the sea among its Scripture parallels: a type of baptism, the passage figuring the conversion of souls and the Egyptians' perdition the ruin of the impenitent. He distinguishes two signs, the instituted sign of the outstretched hand, which showed the thing done in answer to prayer, and the natural sign of a strong east wind, which showed it done by the power of God, whom the winds and seas obey — for the God of nature has not tied himself to nature's laws, but dispenses with them when he pleases. Gill notes the rod was in the hand as directed, and that what the poets say of Bacchus, whose rod was lifted upon the rivers, is truer of Moses, whose had been raised over Egypt's rivers and now over the Red Sea. Calvin admires the restraint of the telling: Moses uses no ornament of language, and the bare recital is the more powerful for it.

What the east wind did is the question. Clarke argues it cannot have divided the waters at all: at the crossing the sea runs some fourteen fathoms deep, and a wind able to lift that mass out of its bed would have blown six hundred thousand people away with it. He concludes that God parted the waters by sovereign power, and that the east wind, always noted as parching, came afterwards to dry the bed — God honouring nature where it can act, and acting alone where it cannot. Ellicott offers the opposite reconstruction. If the Bitter Lakes were joined to the sea by a narrow shallow channel, a south-east wind driving the lake water north while the ebb tide drew the sea water south would leave a stretch of channel dry until the wind shifted; Scripture says nothing of the tide because there was nothing unusual in it, but an Egyptian tradition has Moses waiting for the ebb; whether God carried nature further, he says we are not told. Calvin holds both ends: God could have dispelled the waters without any motion of air, and raised the wind only to show that all nature obeys him — yet no wind could have dried that sea without the secret power of the Spirit beyond nature's ordinary course. Keil declines to fix the quarter, since Hebrew has words only for the four points and the place of the crossing is unknown.

On the ground they crossed the accounts differ. Henry and Wesley make it a bay two or three leagues over; Clarke, on Bruce's authority, about four, easily crossed in a night. Keil explains the dividing as a flowing away of the water to north and south, leaving the bed dry in the middle, the heaped water standing as a wall on either side; Henry notes the wall is mentioned twice, and that the pillar behind kept the Egyptians from charging their flank.

The march itself Henry and Wesley imagine. Moses and Aaron, they suppose, ventured first into the untrodden path and Israel followed; and this would make the later march through the wilderness seem less formidable, for those who had followed God through the sea need not fear to follow him anywhere. They note that it was night, and no moonshine night either, being seven days past the full, so the people had no light but the pillar's — the more awful for that, though where God leads us he will light us. Calvin agrees the pillar made the passage convenient enough by night, and reckons the time from evening to dawn, since so vast a multitude could not have crossed in an hour. He ends on the modesty of the narrator: told to divide the sea with his uplifted rod, Moses changes the expression when he writes it, saying the waters went back at God's command, content with a minister's character and leaving God alone the author.
22:
Whether the wall of waters must be taken literally sets Clarke and Ellicott against each other. Clarke makes the verse the proof of the miracle: had the crossing been managed by an extraordinary ebb, there could have been no waters standing on the right hand and the left, still less standing as a wall against every law of fluids while Israel passed and turning obedient to gravity the moment the Egyptians entered; and he thinks it intolerable that men who receive this as revelation should labour to prove it had nothing miraculous in it. Ellicott answers from usage: a wall in Scripture means any protection whatever, and here the waters covered Israel on either flank; the poets heightened it and spoke of waters standing in a heap, but to build on that the claim that the water congealed into a hard substance, as Kalisch does, is to turn poetry into prose. Gill reports a third question, whether they crossed at all — Aben Ezra and others holding that they went in some way, took a semicircle and came out on the same shore.

Gill sets out the four watches and puts the morning watch between three and six; Clarke adds Calmet's reckoning of about four; Ellicott has it between two and six. On the Lord's looking, Clarke supposes the cloud suddenly took a fiery appearance, or that the Egyptians were appalled by the thunder, lightning and driving rain the psalmist records, tempests enough to terrify the horses and throw the column into confusion. Wesley says the same in brief, terrible winds and lightnings, and terror of mind besides. Calvin reads it as a deliberate opening of their eyes, that too late they might see where their mad impetuosity had brought them and perceive that they contended not with men but with God; struck with that astonishment they could not make the shore in time.

On the wheels Gill collects the guesses: the Targum has them cut off, some think them broken by hailstones, Jarchi that fire burnt them. Wesley turns it into a sentence: they had driven furiously and now drove heavily, their wheels dropping off and the axle-trees failing — they had flown on the back of Israel as the hawk upon the dove, and now cried out to flee. Keil explains the return mechanically: the east wind having ceased, the water flowed together from north and south, and a west wind drove the waves into the faces of the fleeing Egyptians. Ellicott times the order as soon as Israel was across, and describes the end — the white-crested waves advancing on both sides, the chariot wheels clogged, men and horses weighed down with armour, and the flood upon them while they were still far from shore.

Calvin finds a purpose in the daylight: the waters had been heaped in the night, but it was fitting that the Egyptians should perish by day and the sun make their destruction visible, while God urged on their very flight, as though they drowned themselves on purpose. He has no patience with the historians who explained the whole by the tides of the gulf. Whether Pharaoh himself drowned Ellicott treats as an open question, settled by general considerations rather than by this verse. He notes that only the chariots and cavalry entered the sea, so the king might have stayed with the reserve; that had he been killed the silence of Scripture and of the Egyptian annals would be strange; and that Menephthah, to whom the indications point, reigned at least eight years and once declined to lead his army against a Libyan invasion, pleading that the god forbade him to leave Memphis. Wesley has no doubt, and buries him in the deep as a perpetual monument of divine justice; Clarke reports from Josephus fifty thousand horse and two hundred thousand foot, of whom not one was left to carry the news.
30:
Gill dates the salvation precisely. Though it was six or seven days since they had departed, they could not properly be said to be saved until this day, when all the enemies that pursued them were destroyed; and this was the twenty-first of the month, the seventh and last day of the passover, a holy convocation to the Lord. Wesley reads the bodies on the shore as studied contempt: the Egyptians were very curious in preserving the bodies of their great men, and here the grandees of Egypt lie heaps upon heaps, as dung upon the face of the earth. Clarke draws a practical inference — by the extraordinary agitation of the waters multitudes were cast up, and from their spoils Israel was probably furnished with riches, and especially with clothing and arms, essential afterwards in the wars with the Amalekites, Basanites and Amorites; if they did not get their arms this way, we do not know how they got them, since there is no reason to believe they brought any out of Egypt. Ellicott takes the verse as evidence of authorship: on one who saw the sight it would make a great impression, but to later generations it was nothing, since it had no further consequences, so that its being recorded at all indicates the pen of an eyewitness.

On the great work, Gill notes the word is properly hand, and that Israel considered the power which turned the waters that had divided for their safety back upon their pursuers. Keil calls it the might Jehovah had displayed upon Egypt, and distinguishes two ends that do not exclude each other: besides the glory gotten upon Pharaoh promised earlier in the chapter, the passage through the sea was designed to establish Israel more firmly in fear and in faith, so that they should discern not only their merciful deliverer but the holy Judge of the ungodly. Calvin finds the same double aspect in the spectacle, there being no difficulty in distinguishing wrath from fatherly love where an unwarlike multitude was so miraculously preserved and an army formidable on every account destroyed in the depths.

Gill describes it as an awe of his greatness upon their minds and a sense of his goodness upon their hearts, working a filial and godly fear, with belief that he is faithful to his word, able to do all things, and wise to do them in the fittest season. Calvin takes fear here for the reverence that kept them in the way of duty, since they were not merely struck with dread but drawn to devote themselves to a goodness they had so sweetly experienced; believed he reads as added expositively, marking the principal part of that reverence. Clarke has them convinced his power was unlimited both in judgment and in mercy, and satisfied that not one thing had failed of all the good spoken concerning them.

Whether the frame lasted divides them. Wesley says they were now ashamed of their distrusts, and in the mind they were then in would never again despair nor talk of returning to Egypt — adding how well it were for us if we were always in as good a frame as we are sometimes. Calvin grants the affection was general, the recognition of God's hand bowing them to obedience, but holds the ardour soon passed from the greater number, who are moved only by what is visible and present, while some seed remained in a few. Keil and Calvin both tie faith in the Lord to faith in Moses: the miracle was wrought through his hand and staff, and since God willed his words to be heard from that mouth, the mediator could not be despised without God's authority being rejected — from which Calvin draws the rule that those who faithfully deliver God's commands are to be attended to as if he had openly descended from heaven.
